parakeet: The myths allow parents to manage behavior through unseen oversight. The same way God watches everything you do, so does Santa. This keeps children in line long before abstract theology can make sense to them. In non-believing households, the same figures might appear, but they're usually treated differently as stories, not realities. Parents might tell the Santa tale but reveal the truth when children ask. They may do the cultural play. Kids may join the Easter egg hunt or write letters to Santa, but the parents don't embed these myths into the framework of morality, obedience, or reality. Non-believing parents may encourage creativity but prioritize honesty and grounding over prolonged deception. Ultimately, these benevolent myths do more than just entertain. They train children to live inside systems where the unseen governs their lives. Reward and punishment are invisible. You don't see Santa watching, but you know he is. You don't see God judging, but you're told he does. Your transactions with the unseen become normalized. A tooth becomes money, a prayer becomes answered blessing, and then authority validates the myth. If parents insist the tooth fairy is real, a child believes them. If parents insist that Santa Claus is real, a child believes them. Later, when those same parents insist that God and Jesus are real, the same trust carries over. It's soft conditioning, learning to accept without question the promises of unseen powers.
